prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Marathon Petroleum Corp" (ticker MPC), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "MPC", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",

           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?

Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Marathon Petroleum Corporation
result.industry: Oil refining, fuel marketing and midstream
markets: US refined fuels (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel) wholesale
Branded fuel supply to gas stations (Marathon and ARCO brands)
Midstream pipelines, terminals and natural gas processing (MPLX)

mission.plain: Its published tagline is that it is in the business of "accelerating life's possibilities" by supplying the fuel people and businesses depend on; it does not publish a formal mission statement.

about.plain: Marathon Petroleum is the biggest oil refiner in the United States. It buys crude oil and cooks it in 13 huge factories, called refineries, into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. It sells that fuel to gas stations, airlines, trucking companies and other fuel sellers. It also owns most of MPLX, a company with pipelines and storage tanks that move oil and natural gas around the country.
about.customers: Gas station owners, fuel distributors, airlines, trucking and industrial companies, and other energy companies buy its fuels and pipeline services.
about.everyday: When you fill up at a Marathon or ARCO gas station, the gasoline very likely came from one of its refineries.

money.plain: gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other refined products
moving, storing and processing oil and natural gas for fees
diesel made from soybean oil, fats and used cooking oil

result.summary: Marathon Petroleum has a real but limited advantage: it is the largest US refiner (2,986 thousand barrels per calendar day across 13 refineries, about 16% of US capacity) and its plants and logistics give it scale and feedstock flexibility that a newcomer could not replicate, since no large new US refinery has been built in decades. Its product is a commodity priced by crack spreads it does not control, so profits swing widely, but the fee-based MPLX midstream business adds steadier cash flow.

pricingPower.evidence: Fuel prices are set by global crude and product markets, not by MPC: its R&M margin went from $17.58 per barrel in Q2 2025 to $36.33 in Q2 2026 purely because crack spreads jumped during the US-Iran conflict, while its full-year net margin fell from 8.2% in 2022 to 2.5% in 2024 as spreads normalized.

moats.evidence: Marathon (7,882 jobber outlets in 40 states) and ARCO (1,162 direct dealer sites, mainly Southern California) are known brands, but drivers mostly buy fuel on price and convenience.
Wholesale fuel buyers can switch suppliers easily; only long-term brand supply contracts and MPLX's pipeline and gathering agreements create some stickiness.
More customers do not make its fuel more valuable to other customers.

As the largest US refiner, with Galveston Bay the largest US refinery on a stream-day basis (678,000 b/sd per EIA), it spreads fixed costs and runs complex plants that process cheaper heavy and sour crudes; Q2 2026 refining operating costs were $5.72 per barrel.

US refining capacity is shrinking (18.2 million b/cd on Jan 1, 2026, down about 1% after the LyondellBasell Houston and Phillips 66 Los Angeles closures), and permitting makes new refineries and pipelines very hard to build, protecting incumbents' regional positions.
Its model is the same as other large refiners' and offers nothing incumbents cannot copy.
It runs refineries reliably (94% crude utilization in Q2 2026, 97% a year earlier), but peers such as Valero operate at similar levels.

Its integrated asset base, especially MPLX's pipelines, terminals and about 11.2 billion cubic feet per day of gas processing capacity plus Gulf Coast export access, would be nearly impossible to permit and build today.

customers.evidence: Customers are mainly wholesale and branded jobbers on long-term supply agreements, which keeps Marathon and ARCO branded outlets steady (7,882 and 1,162 locations at end-2025), but loyalty is driven by supply reliability and price rather than satisfaction scores; no NPS data is published.

talent.evidence: About 18,500 employees at end-2025 in well-paid, skilled refinery and engineering jobs, but it does not appear on major best-employer rankings and the fossil-fuel industry has trouble attracting younger talent.

product.evidence: Gasoline and diesel are standardized commodities that meet the same specifications as rivals'; its edge is reliable supply and logistics rather than a better product.

competitors.name: Valero Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Second-largest US refiner; competes in Gulf Coast, Mid-Continent and West Coast fuels, exports and renewable diesel (Diamond Green Diesel).

competitors.name: Phillips 66
competitors.note: Large refiner with Phillips 66, 76 and Conoco brands plus midstream and chemicals; closed its Los Angeles refinery in 2025.

competitors.name: Exxon Mobil Corporation
competitors.note: Third-largest US refiner (Baytown, Beaumont, Baton Rouge) with Exxon and Mobil branded stations.

competitors.name: Chevron Corporation
competitors.note: Major West Coast and Gulf Coast refiner and Chevron/Texaco fuel marketer, direct rival to ARCO in California.

competitors.name: Motiva Enterprises
competitors.note: Saudi Aramco-owned operator of Port Arthur, the largest US refinery by calendar-day capacity, and Shell-branded fuel supply in the Gulf and East.

competitors.name: PBF Energy Inc.
competitors.note: Independent refiner competing on the East, Gulf and West Coasts (Martinez, Torrance).

competitors.name: HF Sinclair Corporation
competitors.note: Mid-Continent and Rockies refiner with Sinclair-branded stations and renewable diesel.

competitors.name: Citgo Petroleum Corporation
competitors.note: Refiner in Lake Charles, Lemont and Corpus Christi with Citgo-branded stations in the Midwest and Gulf.

competitors.name: Koch Industries (Flint Hills Resources)
competitors.note: Private refiner in Minnesota and Texas competing for Midwest and Gulf fuel sales.

competitors.name: Shell plc
competitors.note: Shell-branded US fuel retail network and Gulf Coast refining and chemicals.

competitors.name: BP p.l.c.
competitors.note: Whiting (Indiana) refinery and BP/Amoco stations compete directly in MPC's Midwest heartland.

competitors.name: Delek US Holdings, Inc.
competitors.note: Smaller inland refiner in Texas, Louisiana and Arkansas.

competitors.name: CVR Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Mid-Continent refiner in Kansas and Oklahoma.

competitors.name: Neste Oyj
competitors.note: World's largest renewable diesel producer and MPC's 50/50 partner in Martinez Renewables, but a competitor in renewable fuels elsewhere.

competitors.name: Energy Transfer LP
competitors.note: Competes with MPLX in natural gas gathering, processing and pipelines.

marketShare.measure: operable crude distillation capacity (barrels per calendar day)

threats: Crack spreads normalizing after the 2026 Middle East supply shock, which drove Q2 2026 R&M margin to $36.33/bbl versus $17.58 a year earlier
Long-term decline in US gasoline demand from electric vehicles and better fuel economy
New export-oriented refineries in the Middle East, Africa (Dangote) and Asia competing for global product markets
Stricter climate rules, Renewable Fuel Standard compliance costs and California policies hostile to refining
Refinery outages, fires or accidents at large single sites such as Galveston Bay
Weaker renewable diesel economics if tax credits or feedstock costs move against it
Heavy consolidated debt ($32,816M at June 30, 2026, mostly at MPLX) if cash flows fall

ceo.name: Maryann Mannen
ceo.background: Career finance executive: MPC CFO from 2021 and president from January 2024; previously EVP and CFO of TechnipFMC and CFO of FMC Technologies (2007-2017)

c1.evidence: MPC leads US refining by capacity, but refining is a mature, shrinking industry (US capacity fell about 1% in 2025 to 18.2 million b/cd), not an emerging fast-growing one.

c2.evidence: Buyers choose MPC for reliable supply from 13 refineries and MPLX logistics; that asset base is hard to replicate, but the fuel itself is a commodity that rivals sell at the same price.

c3.evidence: Many drivers know the Marathon and ARCO station brands and MPC is the largest US refiner, but it is not a default consumer brand people recommend the way they do Google or Costco.

c4.evidence: MPC publishes only a tagline ("accelerating life's possibilities") and values, and management messaging centres on capital returns and safe operations rather than a mission that would change the world.

c6.evidence: “big oil, gas stations, refineries, pollution”: the public sees it as a large fuel refiner, an impression that is neutral to negative because of environmental concerns and fuel prices.

c7.evidence: US refined fuel demand is large but flat to declining as EVs and fuel efficiency grow; MPC's sales fell from $177,453M in 2022 to $132,699M in 2025.

c8.evidence: Expansion options are mainly MPLX natural gas and NGL growth (2026 growth capex raised to $2.9B for Gulf Coast fractionation) and renewable diesel, not big new markets.

m1.evidence: Maryann Mannen is a disciplined finance executive focused on operational excellence and capital return, not a visionary with a new picture of the future.

m2.evidence: She is a hired professional manager who became CEO in August 2024 after serving as CFO and president, not a founder.

m4.evidence: She emphasizes safety and reliability ("safe and reliable operations to meet resilient consumer demand" in Q2 2026), but there is little public evidence of a distinctive servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: MPC's culture is built on safety, reliability and cost discipline, not on inventing new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Mannen's background is finance (CFO roles at FMC Technologies, TechnipFMC and MPC), not engineering or hands-on product work.

m7.evidence: No public controversies are known, but there is little public record on her personal causes beyond the company's stated values of safety, integrity and environmental stewardship.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Mannen giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: She keeps a low public profile typical of a corporate CFO-turned-CEO.

m9.evidence: Under her leadership MPC reported Q2 2026 net income of $5,138M ($17.73 per diluted share, beating the consensus estimate) with 94% crude utilization, and continued heavy buybacks ($3,283M in H1 2026).

m10.evidence: MPC stresses cost control (refining operating costs of $5.72 per barrel in Q2 2026) and capital discipline, but it is not known for Bezos-style frugality.

c10.evidence: Its fuels power cars, trucks and planes for millions of people across 40+ states and export markets, but it does not transform lives the way NFLX or ISRG do.

p2.evidence: Running 13 complex refineries safely is hard and fuels are essential, but many companies worldwide can do it.

f1.evidence: Sales rose from $69,779M (2020) to $177,453M (2022), then fell each year to $132,699M (2025).

f2.evidence: Operating income fell from $21,469M in 2022 to $8,291M in 2025, so operating margin dropped from 12.1% to 6.2%; margins track crack spreads rather than rising steadily.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive ($25,720M at June 30, 2026) and MPC-standalone debt is $7,176M, but consolidated debt of $32,816M far exceeds $7,768M of cash.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from a $12,247M loss in 2020 to $8,291M in 2025 but peaked at $21,469M in 2022; operating cash flow was $16,361M in 2022 versus $8,253M in 2025.

v1.evidence: Its gasoline and diesel meet the same specifications as rivals', so there is no product reason an ordinary driver would choose it over a Valero, Shell or Exxon station.

v2.evidence: MPC does not appear on major best-places-to-work rankings such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: If MPC vanished, Midwest and Gulf Coast fuel supply would tighten and prices would spike for drivers, truckers and airlines, but other refiners would eventually fill the gap.
